abstract_sentences.text: Token attribution methods provide intuitive explanations for language model outputs by identifying causally important input tokens.

However, as modern LLMs increasingly rely on extended reasoning chains, existing schemes face two critical challenges: (1) efficiency bottleneck, where attributing a target span of M tokens within a context of length N requires O(M · N) operations, making long-context attribution prohibitively slow; and (2) faithfulness drop, where intermediate reasoning tokens absorb attribution mass, preventing importance from propagating back to the original input.

To address these, we introduce FlashTrace, an efficient multi-token attribution method that employs span-wise aggregation to compute attribution over multi-token targets in a single pass, while maintaining faithfulness.
Moreover, we design a recursive attribution mechanism that traces importance through intermediate reasoning chains back to source inputs.

Extensive experiments on long-context retrieval (RULER) and multi-step reasoning (MATH, MorehopQA) tasks demonstrate that FlashTrace achieves over 130× speedup over existing baselines while maintaining superior faithfulness.
We further analyze the dynamics of recursive attribution, showing that even a single recursive hop improves faithfulness by tracing importance through the reasoning chain.
Our code is available at https://github.com/wbopan/flashtrace.

limitations.name: Informational versus causal score
limitations.description: The L1 proximity score measures representation contribution; perturbation evaluation is the paper's separate causal-faithfulness check.

evidence.anchor: rather than a direct causal effect

limitations.name: Residual target-length term
limitations.description: Appendix B keeps scalar O(M·N) attention aggregation, although it treats it as lightweight relative to vector work.

limitations.name: Attention-map cache
limitations.description: Explicit attention maps require O(L·N²) space; on-the-fly recomputation trades compute for memory.

limitations.name: Semantic cancellation
limitations.description: Opposing token semantics can partially cancel before proximity; the paper records it as a caveat even though experiments did not show damage.

limitations.name: Diffuse evidence
limitations.description: Many weakly contributing tokens can diffuse attribution and leave important evidence outside top ranks.

limitations.name: Structural-token salience
limitations.description: Formatting or connective tokens can receive attribution beyond their semantic role due to residual-stream participation.

limitations.name: Uncertainty reporting
limitations.description: Main RISE/MAS/Recovery tables provide no seeds, intervals, or significance test; Table 9 prints ± without defining its statistic.

limitations.name: Deployment evaluation
limitations.description: The paper evaluates benchmarked attribution rather than an end-to-end agent deployment or operator decision study.

adverse_presentation_strategies.description: Main evaluation retains correct answers before random sampling; Appendix K later removes the filter for HotpotQA RISE/MAS. This is an explicit selection condition, not an inference about author intent.

adverse_presentation_strategies.description: For baselines, scores on T/O are discarded and I is renormalized before ranking metrics. This focuses the comparison on source-input rank but changes the direct attribution distribution.

adverse_presentation_strategies.description: Perturbation baselines operate on sentences/chunks and RISE/MAS use 20 five-percent deletion steps. This controls cost and changes resolution from token-by-token procedures.

final_judgment.single_storyline: Reasoning tokens create a local attribution sink; FlashTrace aggregates an output span before expensive vector work and recursively retargets important reasoning tokens to recover source-input importance at practical cost.
final_judgment.main_body_keeps: The motivation diagnosis, Figure 2 mechanism map, Eq. 5–12, Table 1–5, and Figure 4–5 retain the decisions needed to judge the core efficiency/faithfulness claim.
final_judgment.appendix_moves: Algorithmic normalization, precise complexity, baseline adaptations, dataset filtering, metric schedule, hardware, additional long-context checks, resource trade-offs, aggregation alternatives, and failure analysis move to Appendix A–N.
final_judgment.best_pattern: Figure 1 diagnoses the causal break; Figure 2 makes the two-part intervention legible; equations specify it; Table 1/Figure 4 then connect the same intervention to quality and scale.
final_judgment.largest_gap: The broad faithfulness claim rests largely on point-estimate deletion metrics after correctness filtering and modified perturbation schedules; the main O(N) phrasing also abstracts away the Appendix-B scalar M·N term and attention-cache boundary.
final_judgment.transfer_rule: When intermediate generations obscure original evidence, use one diagnostic to isolate the break, then align method diagram, factorization, recursive mechanism, and task evidence to that same break; call each appendix dependency explicitly.
final_judgment.transfer_boundary: This pattern is useful when one mechanism links the observed failures. Diffuse evidence, semantic cancellation, structural-token salience, hidden system state, or missing causal labels require a coarser claim or finer-grained validation.
final_judgment.body_self_sufficiency: The main body explains the method and headline evidence, but evaluation interpretation and exact computational scope depend materially on appendices B–F and K–N.
final_judgment.most_effective_visual_pattern: Use a conceptual full-width mechanism figure before the formal derivation, then reserve a dense results page for the metric matrix and scaling curves.
final_judgment.reader_cost: Readers must traverse a 16-page appendix to reconstruct the actual complexity, baseline treatment, sample filter, metric discretization, and failure modes.

evidence_coverage.coverage_note: Physical PDF pages 1–26 were read; every inventory item and judgment has one or more page/section anchors. References were read as document boundary material, not used to infer method facts.
